---
title: "Quiz: Lucas–Kanade"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Convention: $x$ to the right, $y$ down; flow in pixels per frame.

---

**Q1.** What does Lucas–Kanade assume, and how does that assumption get around the aperture problem?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many constraint lines does a window give?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It assumes the flow is the same for all pixels of a small window. Then the window gives many constraint lines for the same two unknowns; if the gradients in the window point in different directions, the lines cross and the velocity is determined (least squares: the point closest to all lines).
:::

---

**Q2.** The Lucas–Kanade matrix of a window has eigenvalues 300 and 280. Another window has 300 and 0.5, a third 0.4 and 0.1. Where would you trust the flow?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
It is the [structure tensor](../structure-tensor/lec.qmd) of the edges day.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
First window (both large): a corner or texture, trust it. Second (one large, one tiny): an edge, only the motion across the edge is reliable. Third (both tiny): flat, no information. The smaller eigenvalue $\mu_2$ is the confidence.
:::

---

**Q3.** You double the window radius ρ. Name one thing that gets better and one that gets worse.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Noise, and what lies inside the window.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Better: more pixels average the noise away and fewer windows contain only one edge. Worse: the window reaches across motion boundaries and mixes different motions (a cell and the still background), and fine detail of the flow field is blurred.
:::

---

**Q4.** Lucas–Kanade gives nonsense for a shift of 8 pixels on the micrograph. Why? Give two remedies.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The constraint is a first-order Taylor expansion.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The linearisation holds only for motion small compared with how fast the gradient changes (about a pixel at the scale of the image structure). Remedies: iterate with warping (estimate, warp frame 2 back, estimate the rest), and go coarse to fine on a Gaussian pyramid, where 8 px is 1 px at level 3.
:::

---

**Q5.** On a 4-level pyramid (levels 0 to 3), the true motion is 12 px. What is it at each level? When going from level 2 to level 1, what do you do with the flow found at level 2?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each level halves the pixel count per side.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
12, 6, 3 and 1.5 px at levels 0, 1, 2, 3. Going from level 2 to level 1: upsample the flow to the finer grid and **double** it (a pixel at level 2 is two pixels at level 1), warp frame 2 by it, and estimate the remaining small motion.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why does block matching cope with large motion while Lucas–Kanade does not? What does Lucas–Kanade do better?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Searching vs linearising.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Block matching tries every shift in a search range and keeps the best score, so it does not depend on a linearisation. But it gives integer shifts unless a peak is fitted, and is slow (many shifts per window). Lucas–Kanade is sub-pixel by construction and cheap (five blurs and a $2\times2$ solve per pixel).
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* Write the normal equations of Lucas–Kanade for a window. What happens when all gradients in the window are parallel?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Differentiate $\sum w(I_xu + I_yv + I_t)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\begin{pmatrix}\sum wI_x^2 & \sum wI_xI_y\\ \sum wI_xI_y & \sum wI_y^2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix} = -\begin{pmatrix}\sum wI_xI_t\\ \sum wI_yI_t\end{pmatrix}$. With all gradients parallel to a unit vector $\mathbf n$, $J = c\,\mathbf n\mathbf n^\top$ has rank 1 (determinant 0): only $\mathbf n \cdot \mathbf u$ is determined; the minimum-norm solution is the normal flow.
:::
